imageInfo.caption: Charles of Anjou enthroned with crown and sceptre, in a marble statue carved in his lifetime by Arnolfo di Cambio around 1277, now in the Capitoline Museums in Rome.
imageInfo.creator: Arnolfo di Cambio (sculptor); photograph by Wilfredo Rodriguez (Wilfredor)
imageInfo.source: Capitoline Museums, Rome (inv. S 830); photograph via Wikimedia Commons, CC0
imageInfo.note: Marble, about 160 cm high, Musei Capitolini inventory S 830 (Wikidata). Arnolfo carved it around 1277, while Charles was Senator of Rome. It is counted among the earliest realistic portraits of a living person in post-classical sculpture. Italian Wikipedia says it once stood in Santa Maria in Aracoeli; its original setting and any later restorations were not checked against the museum catalogue.

overview: Charles of Anjou was brother of Louis IX, king of Sicily, and a Mediterranean ruler whose ambitions linked crusading, papal policy, Italy, and plans against Byzantium.
His legacy is controversial: a crusading and papal champion to some, an aggressive dynastic conqueror to others.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Charles of Anjou was brother of Louis IX, king of Sicily, and a Mediterranean ruler whose ambitions linked crusading, papal policy, Italy, and plans against Byzantium.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Charles was born into the Capetian royal family and gained power through appanage, marriage, papal alliance, and conquest.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Charles of Anjou is remembered as a cold, austere, and overwhelmingly ambitious ruler, a man of relentless drive who built a Mediterranean empire and pursued grand designs with ruthless determination. The sources present a stern, hard-working, and humourless prince — brother of Saint Louis but utterly unlike him in temperament — who conquered the Kingdom of Sicily, executed his young rival Conradin, and dreamed of restoring the Latin Empire and dominating the eastern Mediterranean.

His severity and the heavy hand of his rule provoked the famous uprising of the Sicilian Vespers in 1282, which shattered his ambitions and revealed how widely his harsh, tax-heavy administration was hated. The chroniclers present a ruler of formidable energy and discipline whose lack of warmth and political flexibility ultimately undid his grandest projects.

What the record consistently conveys is a man of iron ambition and cold efficiency, admired for his capability and feared for his ruthlessness. He is remembered as the austere empire-builder of the central Mediterranean — tireless, calculating, and grim — whose overreaching ambition and harsh rule brought him both a crown and, in the Vespers, a humbling reversal.

contentSections.title: As Angevin Mediterranean ruler
paragraphs: Charles conquered the Hohenstaufen kingdom of Sicily with papal backing and became a major force in crusading politics. His ambitions toward Constantinople and the eastern Mediterranean were checked by the Sicilian Vespers.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Charles died in 1285 after the Vespers shattered much of his Mediterranean project.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy is controversial: a crusading and papal champion to some, an aggressive dynastic conqueror to others.
